sentences.text: The pond is not much and Elin would like that clear, because people hear about it and imagine somewhere.

It is about forty metres across and it is in a dip in a field below the farm, and it has reeds along the north side and a willow that came down in 2015 and has gone on growing lying down, and it has a wooden thing at one end that was a jetty in about 1970 and is now four posts.
Her family have farmed above it since 1911.
Elin has swum in it.
Her father learned to swim in it.
There are newts in it and in April there is frogspawn and in a hot July it smells.
It is on the farm's land and nobody outside the family has been down there in years.
There is no path to it and no sign and no reason for anybody to go, and the gate at the top of the field has been tied with the same orange baler twine since about 2012.

The dragonfly is a golden-ringed and it is the largest species in Britain, which is not saying an enormous amount — about eight centimetres — and it is black with yellow bands and green eyes that meet in the middle.
There is one on that pond every summer.
Not the same one.

Elin is entirely clear about this and gets slightly short with people who want it to be the same one: a golden-ringed dragonfly lives as an adult for a few weeks and spends the previous two to five years as a larva in the mud, and there is no version of the biology in which an insect on that pond in 1994 is an insect on that pond in 2024.
What is the same is the reed.
Elin has thought about whether that is even remarkable and has decided it probably is not.
A dragonfly perch is a position, not a plant: a stem that stands clear at a particular height with a particular view of the water and the sun behind it in the afternoon.
If the geometry of a pond stays the same, the best perch stays the same, and a reed clump on a bank stays where it is for decades.
That is almost certainly the whole of it.
It lands on the same reed.
Third from the left of the clump at the north end, about sixty centimetres up, facing the water.

Elin has counted from the left every time and has been careful to count from the same end, which sounds obvious and which she got wrong twice before she made herself write down which end the willow was at.

Elin has photographs from four different summers and her father has one from about 1996 that his mother took, and it is the same reed clump and it is very nearly the same position within it, and Elin has no explanation for this at all and does not think it is the interesting part.
